subject: Biology
title: Transcription: Copying the Code
description: A quick, practical guide to Transcription: Copying the Code.

hook.text: To use a gene, the cell first copies it from DNA into messenger RNA. This is transcription.

buildup.text: RNA polymerase unzips a section of DNA and builds an RNA strand matching the gene.

discovery.text: Only one strand of DNA is read. The other strand stays as a backup template.

twist.text: Before leaving the nucleus, the RNA is edited—introns are cut out, exons are spliced together.

climax.text: The finished mRNA exits through nuclear pores and heads for the ribosomes.

punchline.text: Copy the gene, edit the script, send it out.

quiz.question: What enzyme builds the RNA strand during transcription?

details.summary: Transcription is the process of copying a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA. RNA polymerase reads the template strand and constructs a complementary mRNA molecule that carries the genetic instructions from the nucleus to ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
details.whyItMatters: Transcription is the first step in gene expression and a primary point of regulation. Cells control which genes are transcribed and when, making transcription the gatekeeper between the genome's potential and its actual use.
takeaways: RNA polymerase binds the promoter region to initiate transcription
The mRNA strand is complementary to the DNA template strand
Pre-mRNA is processed by splicing, capping, and adding a poly-A tail

faq.question: What starts and stops transcription?
faq.answer: Transcription begins when transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble at the gene's promoter sequence. It stops when the polymerase reaches a terminator sequence, releasing the completed mRNA strand from the DNA template.

faq.question: What is mRNA splicing?
faq.answer: Newly transcribed pre-mRNA contains both coding regions (exons) and non-coding regions (introns). Splicing removes introns and joins exons together. Alternative splicing can join different exon combinations, allowing one gene to produce multiple protein variants.
